name: Zoe Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you privately think. What is your normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 43, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I help wire homes and repair business premises, with a senior worker checking my work because I'm still slower and less skilled than the others. Today I prepared fittings in a small office and needed a second demonstration before I got the spacing right. I like a finished row looking proper; I don't like being asked to hurry past something I haven't understood.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your situation away from work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs household appliances, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn a typical trade wage, we have four months of expenses saved, and there are some other electrical firms nearby. I never use AI tools and prefer a marked drawing and somebody showing me the work. I believe in learning a proper trade, paying our own way and helping family; I'd rather try a paid apprenticeship route than buy a promise about a new career.

say: I'd welcome fewer **grand announcements** and let the office improve invoices while we did the practical work.
I'd still ask for a **demonstration** before being expected to understand an unfamiliar task.
think: Our **work and bills** look steady, with four months of expenses saved and some alternative employers nearby.
I value a **careful day's wage** even while I still need supervision and practice.
do: Continue the usual **supervised fitting** and preparation work now and through the first plateau year.
Keep **marked drawings** and request repeat demonstrations rather than buying tools or leaving over invoice changes.
feel: **Calm** about household money and work, despite ordinary embarrassment when she makes a mistake.
S0.quote: A proper job matters more than saving face.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on ongoing paid work, a moderate reserve and some alternative employers, rather than unusually strong skill.
She accepts **supervision from younger workers** while retaining familiar methods and avoiding new spending based only on reassuring news.

steps.text: Continue supervised fitting and preparation using marked drawings and demonstrations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I wouldn't miss the grand announcements. Let the office tidy the invoices and let us do a proper day's work. I'd still want someone to show me the task before expecting me to know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and bills look steady in that picture, with four months set aside if something ordinary goes wrong. I'm still learning, but I have work, checks and a few other firms around. I don't need a clever machine to make a careful day's wage worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep doing supervised preparation and fitting on the usual jobs. Through the plateau's first year I'd keep my marked drawings and ask for another demonstration whenever I needed one. I wouldn't buy a tool or leave the firm because the office had found a quicker invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household and the work, though I can still get flustered when I make a mistake. I'd feel glad to keep practising the same trade instead of being told to start another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when you make a mistake in front of a younger colleague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior worker what I'd got wrong and do that part again under supervision. I wouldn't hide the mistake because I was older than the person checking it. A proper job matters more than saving face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend more because the AI picture felt quieter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the reserve available rather than spend it because the news had quietened down. That's the money we already put by, not extra income from the scenario. We'd still want it if the washing machine failed.

say: I'd accept office changes while asking for **teaching time** instead of turning every visit into a race.
I'd tell the owner a **faster booking** cannot make a beginner learn a practical task faster.
think: I expect my **paid practical work** to hold while the firm still needs preparation and fitting under checks.
Rushed senior workers could leave me with **less teaching**, even if the normal household wage continues.
do: Record tasks needing **repeat demonstration** and request a weekly paid practice period now.
Continue **supervised work** during the first year and flag visits without enough time for required checks.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed teaching, while expecting the normal wage and mortgage payments to remain secure.
S1.quote: A faster booking doesn't mean a beginner has learned faster.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **teaching pressure** from expected income loss, keeping her own wage secure in this scenario despite discomfort.
Her **practice request** specifies demonstration, repetition and checking during paid hours, without counting an unagreed arrangement as completed training.

steps.text: Continue supervised electrical work and flag visits missing required checking time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can change its tools without turning every visit into a race. I'd ask the owner to leave time for the senior worker to teach me properly. A faster booking doesn't mean a beginner has learned faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my paid work to hold because I'm still needed to carry, prepare and fit things under checks. But I'd be uneasy if the senior worker was rushed from job to job. I don't learn by being left with a screen and told the answer is in there somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep a paper note of tasks where I needed a second demonstration and ask the supervisor for a weekly paid practice period. In the first year I'd continue the same supervised work and flag visits booked without enough checking time. I wouldn't say I had agreed training until the owner actually agreed the paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the pace around the job, while still expecting to bring the normal wage home. I'd be annoyed at being treated as a delay rather than frightened of next month's mortgage. Those aren't the same feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the office required an unfamiliar AI record tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hadn't been taught it and ask who would show me during paid time. I wouldn't start using AI on my own to avoid an awkward conversation. I don't want a neat record that hides a practical mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of teaching arrangement would you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for one named person to show the task, watch me repeat it and check the result. That fits an apprenticeship to me. I'd want the practice to keep my wage intact, not be offered instead of paid site hours.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking changes** from robots around 2031, without promising every junior place survives.
I'd want a **paid route** through the gap rather than reassurance that hands-on work stays safe forever.
think: My **hours could shrink** as firms prepare to keep fewer people for the same practical work.
Four months of **expenses saved** creates some time, without replacing the mortgage contribution my wage provides.
do: Ask the old instructor about actual **paid adult apprenticeships** now.
Take a supervised **apprenticeship place** only if its wage covers household bills after travel.
Apply after 2028 for posted **junior repair roles** with written hours, keeping this job until a signed offer.
feel: **Anxious** about income loss, with a reserve and a practical plan rather than immediate helplessness.
S2.quote: I'd rather ask for paid teaching than pretend a certificate had made me experienced.
fieldNote: Her **apprenticeship route** remains conditional on a livable wage after travel and real supervision, preserving both household and skill constraints.
She favours **family discussion** without assuming a partner replaces lost earnings or relatives promise unlimited childcare.

steps.text: Take supervised adult apprenticeship only if wages cover bills after travel
Apply after 2028 for junior repair roles with written hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew not to call 2028 the day every pair of hands becomes useless. The thinking work changes first, then capable robots follow around 2031. I'd still want a paid route through that gap instead of assuming juniors would be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours as firms prepared to keep fewer people for the same work. Four months of expenses would give us a little time, but my wage still pays a real part of the mortgage. I wouldn't want to be slow at a trade just as the places to practise narrowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my old training instructor about actual paid apprenticeship places for adults. I'd take one before 2028 only if the wage covered our bills after travel and the practical teaching was supervised. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted junior repair roles with written hours, keeping the current job until another offer was signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing income, but not without a plan or money for the next week. I'd hate having to explain that another apprenticeship might be needed. I'd rather ask for paid teaching than pretend a certificate had made me experienced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a paid apprenticeship affordable for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the actual wage and journey for any place before deciding. If it meant an unpaid course or a wage we couldn't live on, I'd keep looking. Family support would mean talking honestly, not assuming my partner could replace my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family for any practical help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a particular school pickup was possible while I attended an actual interview. I wouldn't ask for an unlimited promise or build my work plan around an answer I hadn't got. People in the family have their own days to manage.

say: I'd use **five years** to ask for proper teaching now rather than wait until 2031.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** visible alongside the earlier change to thinking work.
think: I expect my **practical wage** to hold during the next few preparation years while I improve under supervision.
I would still worry about **later change**, because unfamiliar methods take me time to learn.
do: Request regular **paid practice** now without losing site pay.
Take a supervised **adult apprenticeship** before 2031 only if wages cover bills after travel.
Apply after 2031 for posted **junior service jobs** where written wages and hours improve the household position.
feel: **Uneasy** about later changes, while secure about near-term bills and glad of time for repeated practice.
S3.quote: I'd need a written offer before changing work.
fieldNote: She judges **progress** by correctly performed supervised tasks rather than attendance or another qualification name alone.
Her **slower response** remains active but cautious, protecting the present wage until an actual affordable supervised opportunity exists.

steps.text: Take supervised adult apprenticeship only if wages cover bills after travel
Apply after 2031 for junior service jobs with better written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should let someone teach me properly while we're still doing the work. I'd ask for that now, not just wait until the thinking change in 2031. I'd keep the robot date around 2034 in mind as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd expect my practical hours and wage to hold for longer while I learned. That would make the reserve a cushion rather than the first part of a lost wage. I'd still worry about changing direction later because I don't take quickly to unfamiliar things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd request a regular supervised practice period as part of paid work, without losing site pay. I'd take an actual adult apprenticeship before 2031 only if the wage covered bills after travel and the teaching was supervised. In the first year after 2031 I'd compare posted junior service jobs and apply where written terms improved our position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later change, but secure about our bills over the next few years. I'd feel better having time to repeat tasks until I understood them. I wouldn't suddenly become someone who learns from an AI chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge progress during the extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see which tasks I could do correctly under the required checks. A year's attendance without learning the work wouldn't be enough. I'd ask the instructor what I still needed to practise rather than buy another qualification name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer never provided the promised practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present wage while asking about other actual supervised places. We have a mortgage, so leaving to make a point would be a poor use of the reserve. I'd need a written offer before changing work.

say: I'd use **a decade** to learn properly while still asking for paid practice this year.
I'd remind the firm that a **calendar** cannot demonstrate a good electrical connection to a learner.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume the household could stop earning when hands-on robots followed.
Present wages, our **four-month reserve** and some alternative employers make near-term household bills look secure.
do: Request **paid supervised practice** now and review the next practical skill each year.
Take a supervised **adult apprenticeship** before 2036 only with wages covering bills after travel.
Apply after 2036 for posted **repair jobs** matching completed skills, changing only after a signed affordable offer.
feel: **Uneasy** about later career change, while secure about near-term household living and able to learn slowly.
S4.quote: Family responsibility includes not making children carry the parent's work problem.
fieldNote: She makes no **future-income assumptions** from older ages, keeping hoped-for retirement or children's earnings outside the present plan.
Her **annual skill check** creates an earlier trigger to inspect real supervised alternatives if promised teaching never occurs.

steps.text: Take supervised adult apprenticeship only with wages covering bills after travel
Apply for repair jobs matching completed skills and offering affordable written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives a person time to learn a proper trade if the teaching is there. I'd still ask for the paid practice this year. Ten years on a calendar doesn't show somebody how to make a good connection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 56 when hands-on robots followed. I couldn't assume we could stop earning then, even with the children older. But our current wages, four-month reserve and some nearby employers make the next few years look secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request the same paid supervised practice and ask at each review what I should learn next. I'd accept an adult apprenticeship before 2036 only with supervised teaching and wages that covered bills after travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for posted repair jobs matching skills I'd actually gained, leaving only after a signed offer with workable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about needing to change later, but not worried about the household getting through next month. More time would let me learn slowly without giving up. I'd keep the notebook and the habit of asking for a check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep you from waiting through the whole decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask each year which new tasks I could safely do with the required checks and whether they led to paid work. If I was still only being promised teaching, I'd compare other real places earlier. I wouldn't call waiting ten years learning ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the children’s plans now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change their studies from one picture or count their future wages as ours. I'd tell them I was still learning and asking for proper help. Family responsibility includes not making children carry the parent's work problem.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose hours before I'd learned enough to move confidently. A paid apprenticeship with a proper person teaching and a wage we could live on would help. I can admit I need teaching without handing over the mortgage money for a promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what somebody means by being willing to work. I'm willing, but that doesn't mean I can safely do a task nobody has shown me. I'd want a fair chance to learn it properly and earn my way.

headlineQuote: I can admit I need teaching without handing over the mortgage money for a promise.
portrait: **Zoe, 43**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate and practical skills still below the experienced crew's level.
She and **her partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage, typical trade pay and four months of expenses saved near some alternatives.
She **never uses AI**, preferring demonstrations, marked drawings and checked practice while valuing trade work and household responsibility.
Fast competition creates **income anxiety**; slower timelines support careful paid learning without assumed retirement, partner replacement wages or children's future income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut paid hours before she learns enough to move confidently.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** with supervised practical teaching and livable wages would help her earn while learning.
